newsitem.title: USA: Republican governors want relief from welfare bill.
newsitem.headline: Republican governors want relief from welfare bill.

text.p: Republican governors asked Senate leaders Friday for relief from a new welfare law that ends federal aid to hundreds of thousands of legal immigrants, leaving states to pick up a multi-billion-dollar tab.

While pledging to work with the governors, top Senate Republicans publicly held out little hope that Congress would reopen the broad welfare law, which will end Food Stamps and federal disability aid to most legal immigrants this summer.
"We don't see a whole lot more money coming from Uncle Sam," Assistant Senate Majority Leader Don Nickles, an Oklahoma Republican, said after meeting with several Republican state executives.
"I'm concerned about opening up the (welfare) bill before the ink is dry," he said.
Privately Senate Republicans, who requested the meeting, are anxious to find some way to avoid a difficult political split with the governors on the issue.

President Clinton plans to ask Congress to restore some aid to elderly and disabled legal immigrants as part of a package of $13 billion in welfare restorations, to be included in a 1998 budget plan he submits to Congress next month.

The National Governors' Association will also vote on a resolution at its winter meeting in early February taking issue with cuts in aid to elderly and disabled immigrants in the United States prior to the signing of the welfare law.
The immigrant cuts total about $24 billion over six years.

"I think it's inappropriate to change the rules retroactively, to deny benefits to those who came here under the old rules," said New York Republican Gov. George Pataki, one of those meeting with Republican lawmakers.
"The federal government should revisit this particular aspect of the welfare bill," he said.

Pataki estimated 80,000 immigrants would lose aid in his state under the new law. It would cost New York $240 million a year to make up for the federal cut. Illinois Republican Gov. Jim Edgar, another participant, predicted 30,000 immigrants would be hurt in Illinois at an annual cost of $163 million.
Advocacy groups have warned that elderly and disabled immigrants may be turned out of nursing homes or forced into poverty when the cuts take effect this summer.
Rhode Island Republican Gov. Lincoln Almond also attended the meeting at Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott's office.
The meeting focused on elderly and disabled immigrants here prior to August 1996, when Clinton signed the law.

Republican lawmakers plan additional meetings with the governors. They are considering some steps to ease the impact of the bill, including making it easier for long-time immigrants to gain citizenship, which would restore their benefits. They also said they would try to give states more flexibilty to use existing funds under the welfare bill.
The welfare law ends a 60-year guarantee of federal aid to poor women and children, instead giving states block grants to design and run their own welfare programs.

Overall, the law cuts federal spending by $54 billion over five years. About 44 percent of the cuts come from denying Supplemental Security Income, Food Stamps and other federal benefits to legal immigrants.
